---
title: "The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO"
subtitle: "Why so much of Sunday's playbook was invented on Saturday, and what the NFL kept"
description: "How college football became the sport's research lab: the talent gaps, wide hash marks, three-yard ineligible rule, tempo and roster churn that push college coaches to invent; the offensive lineages from the split-T, veer, wishbone and flexbone through the Wing-T, BYU's passing game, the Air Raid, the spread offense, the spread option, the pistol, tempo and the RPO; the defensive answers (the 3-3-5 stack, pattern-matching quarters, tite and mint fronts, three-high safety defenses); when and how each idea crossed into the NFL, with the data on shotgun football; and a side-by-side table of the college and NFL rules that make Saturday and Sunday look different."
glossary:
  "Spread offense": "An offensive philosophy, grown mostly in college football, that lines up in the shotgun with three or four receivers spread across the field to pull defenders out of the box, then attacks the space that leaves with quick passes, option reads or both. A spread formation is the picture; a spread offense is the whole system built on it."
  "Spread option": "A spread offense whose run game is built on option reads from the shotgun or pistol (the zone read and its relatives), so the quarterback's running threat gives the offense an extra man; popularized by Rich Rodriguez and Urban Meyer in the 2000s."
  "3-3-5 stack": "A college defense with three down linemen, three linebackers stacked directly behind them and five defensive backs, two of them hybrid safety-linebackers who align outside the box; built to put speed on the field against spread offenses and to hide which of the stacked players will rush."
  "Three-high safety defense": "A defense that shows three safeties deep before the snap, usually from a 3-3-5, so that eight players can drop into coverage against the pass or one of the safeties can come down after the snap to fill against the run; made famous by Iowa State in 2017 against the Big 12's passing offenses."

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"
#| output: false
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, RegularPolygon, Rectangle
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
import gridiron.field as gfield
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style
from gridiron.field import FIELD_WIDTH

GREEN = "#0f7a55"           # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]    # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
OL = ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """Five offensive linemen, unlabelled (in this chapter 'C' and 'CB' always mean a cornerback)."""
    return [q.moved(label="") for q in offense("gun_2x2") if q.key in OL]


def spread10(rb_w=-2.4, qb_d=-5.0, rb_d=-5.4):
    """Shotgun, four receivers (10 personnel): X and Z on the line, the slots H and F a step off it.
    The back is offset 2.4 yards and a little deeper, so his marker never touches the quarterback's."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", qb_d, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", rb_d, rb_w, "R"),
                      O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                      O("F", "WR", -1.5, 9.0, "F"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0, "Z")]


def check_legal(players):
    """Seven offensive players on the line, and only the two at its ends may be eligible receivers."""
    off = [q for q in players if q.side == "off"]
    on = sorted([q for q in off if q.d > -1.0], key=lambda q: q.w)
    assert len(on) == 7, [q.key for q in on]
    for q in on[1:-1]:
        assert q.key in OL, f"{q.key} is covered up but not a lineman"


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, path, run, route or rush."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed, frame="field")
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run, "pull": p.pull, "rush": p.rush}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def branch(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, label=None, label_at=None, lw=2.0, fontsize=7.5,
           dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed 'option' path through absolute (d, w) points, with an arrowhead (or block tee)."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6, solid_capstyle="round")
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=11, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))
    else:
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)
    if label:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, *(label_at or pts[-1]))
        fld.ax.text(x, y, label, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, fontweight="bold", ha="center",
                    va="center", zorder=9,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=0.8))


def pitch_arc(fld, p, a, b, color=style.BALL, rad=0.25):
    """A pitch or a throw: a dashed brown arc from (d, w) a to (d, w) b."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, *a), _P(fld, p, *b)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                     mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=7,
                                     connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}"))


def read_line(fld, p, a, b, color=GREEN, num=None, at=0.5):
    """The quarterback's eyes: a thin dashed green line between two (d, w) spots, optionally numbered."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, *a), _P(fld, p, *b)
    fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), alpha=0.85, zorder=4)
    if num:
        fld.ax.text(x0 + at * (x1 - x0), y0 + at * (y1 - y0), num, fontsize=7, color="white", ha="center",
                    va="center", fontweight="bold", zorder=9,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.18", fc=color, ec="none"))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def box_shade(fld, p, d0, d1, w0, w1, color=GREEN, alpha=0.07):
    """Shade a rectangle of the field (the 'box') between depths d0-d1 and widths w0-w1."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=color, alpha=alpha,
                               ec=color, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))


def clean(ax, numbers=True, hashes=True):
    """Drop hash ticks and/or painted yard numbers (box-sized windows), clip everything to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if hashes and len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if numbers and t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, numbers=True, hashes=True, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax, numbers=numbers, hashes=hashes)
    return fld


def panel_title(ax, text, size=9):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=size, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


class hashes_at:
    """Temporarily draw gridiron Fields with college hash marks (60 feet, 20 yards, in from each sideline).
    gridiron.field reads HASH_NEAR / HASH_FAR when it draws, so we swap them and put them back."""

    def __init__(self, from_sideline=20.0):
        self.near, self.far = from_sideline, FIELD_WIDTH - from_sideline

    def __enter__(self):
        self.saved = (gfield.HASH_NEAR, gfield.HASH_FAR)
        gfield.HASH_NEAR, gfield.HASH_FAR = self.near, self.far
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        gfield.HASH_NEAR, gfield.HASH_FAR = self.saved
        return False


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- frame strips and videos (as in 03-04)
MARK_R = 0.72


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def carrier(play, t):
    """Who holds the ball at time t (QB until the first handoff, pitch or catch)."""
    holder = "QB"
    for kind, to, te in sorted(play.ball_events, key=lambda e: e[2]):
        if t >= te + (0.35 if kind in ("pitch", "pass") else 0.0):
            holder = to
    return holder


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, trails, the ball, rings (and a ring on the ball carrier)."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.4, play.los + window[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")
                & df["x"].between(play.los + window[0], play.los + window[1])]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.5), 0.75, 0.45, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.8 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.6)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in list(rings) + [(carrier(play, t), style.THIRD)]:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key]
        if len(rr):
            x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"].iloc[0], rr["y"].iloc[0])
            ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.25, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.9, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(plays, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rows=None, rings=(), width_in=6.5, ncols=None):
    """Frame strip: one row per play (an option's branches), or one play wrapped over rows."""
    dfs = [tracking(p) for p in plays]
    if len(plays) > 1:
        cells = [(i, t) for i in range(len(plays)) for t in times]
        ncols = len(times)
    else:
        cells = [(0, t) for t in times]
        ncols = ncols or min(3, len(times))
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(cells) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.55 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(cells):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for k, (ax, (i, t)) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, cells)):
        panel(ax, plays[i], dfs[i], t, lateral, window, rings)
        head = f"{k % len(times) + 1 if len(plays) > 1 else k + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s")
        if rows and k % ncols == 0:
            head = rows[i] + "   " + head
        ax.set_title(head, fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2 if not (rows and k % ncols == 0) else style.INK,
                     loc="left", fontweight="bold" if rows and k % ncols == 0 else "normal")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[k], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.5)
    return fig


def video(plays, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rows=None, rings=(), width_in=6.4):
    """Web version: the same panels drawn at every tenth of a second, side by side for branches."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    dfs = [tracking(p) for p in plays]
    t0 = min(float(df["time"].min()) for df in dfs)
    t1 = max(float(df["time"].max()) for df in dfs)
    grid = np.round(np.arange(t0, t1 + 1e-9, 0.1), 2)
    n = len(plays)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    pw = (width_in if n == 1 else width_in / n) * (0.85 if n == 1 else 1.0)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, squeeze=False, figsize=(pw * n, pw * span_d / span_w + 0.6))
    axes = axes.flat

    def update(t):
        for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
            ax.clear()
            panel(ax, plays[i], dfs[i], t, lateral, window, rings)
            txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
            if notes:
                per = len(times)
                mine = notes[i * per:(i + 1) * per] if n > 1 else notes
                cur = [m for tt, m in zip(times, mine) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
                txt += ("\n" + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""
            head = (rows[i] + ": ") if rows else ""
            ax.set_title(head + txt, fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=list(grid), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def option_animation(plays, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rows=None, rings=(), **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(plays, times, lateral, window, notes=notes, rows=rows, rings=rings, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(plays, times, lateral, window, notes=notes, rows=rows, rings=rings)
```

Saturday night, third-and-6. The offense snaps the ball eleven seconds after the last play ended. Four
receivers stand spread across a field whose hash marks seem to sit almost on the sideline; the ball is on
the left one, and the whole offense seems to have drifted to the wide side of the field. The quarterback,
five yards behind the center, puts the ball in his running back's belly, watches a defensive end, pulls the
ball, takes two steps, and flips it to a slot receiver bowing backward toward the sideline. Twelve yards.
The next afternoon you watch an NFL team run almost the same play: same read, same flip, same receiver.
The NFL version is a little quicker, the line looks a little different, and the announcer calls it "a
college concept." He is right, and he could have said the same thing about half the plays in the game.
Where did they come from, why does college football keep inventing them, and why do some make the jump
to Sunday while others never do?

**You'll be able to:**

- Explain the four forces that make college football the sport's laboratory: talent gaps across hundreds of
  programs, wide hash marks, rules that tolerate the run-pass blur, and roster churn and tempo.
- Trace the main offensive lineages (split-T and veer, wishbone and flexbone, Wing-T, BYU's passing game, the
  Air Raid, the spread offense, the spread option, the pistol, tempo and the RPO) and point to their DNA in an
  NFL play.
- Trace the defensive answers (the 3-3-5 stack, pattern-matching quarters, tite and mint fronts, and the
  three-high safety defense) and say which problem each was built to solve.
- Say when and how each idea crossed into the NFL, and why some never did.
- Read a college broadcast with the rulebook differences in mind (hash width, one foot in bounds, three yards
  downfield, a 15-yard pass-interference cap, the college clock, overtime, targeting and more), and predict
  how each one changes what the teams do.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}

  from the Mel Blount rule and Air Coryell to the West Coast offense and the run-and-shoot. This chapter tells
  the college side of the same decades and carries it forward.
- **[Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd)**: the read key, give and keep, the zone
  read, the inverted veer, the triple option's dive, keep and pitch, and the count (#1 dive key, #2 pitch key,
  #3 alley, #4 deep). This chapter traces where those plays came from rather than re-teaching them.
- **[Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)**: the conflict defender, pre- and post-snap

  college ones.

**How to read the diagrams.** The offense always moves up the page, and *left* and *right* mean the
offense's left and right.

- **Offense** (blue circles): Q quarterback, R running back; X and Z wide receivers on the line, H and F slot
  receivers a step off it, Y a tight end. In the option backfields, F, FB or B is the fullback and H or A a
  halfback or A-back. The linemen are blank circles.
- **Defense** (orange squares): numbers are technique alignments from
  [Run-Game Language](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) (1 = on the center's shoulder; 2i and
  4i = the inside shoulder of the guard and the tackle; 3 and 5 = the outside shoulder of the guard and the
  tackle; 7 = a tight end's inside shoulder). N is a nose tackle; S, M and W the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers; CB a cornerback,
  NB a nickel back; SS and FS the strong and free safeties, and LS and RS the left and right safeties of a
  three-safety shell; SP and BA the 3-3-5's two hybrid safeties (the *spur* and *bandit*).
- **Lines**: a short bar is a block, a thick dark arrow a ball carrier, a dashed arrow one of a play's possible
  *branches*, a dashed brown arc a pitch or a throw, and a thin dashed green line runs from the quarterback to
  the defender he is reading. Orange rings mark defenders to watch.

## Why college invents and the NFL borrows

Watch enough football and a pattern appears. Almost every offensive idea that changed the NFL in the last
thirty years, the shotgun spread run game, the zone read, the pistol, the RPO, the spread no-huddle, the Air
Raid's handful of pass concepts, arrived from college (the NFL had flirted with the no-huddle in the K-Gun
era; college made it an identity), often a decade or more after it was born there. The
traffic runs the other way much less often. That isn't because college coaches are smarter. It is because
college football is a different *environment*, and four features of that environment reward invention.

### 1. More teams, and bigger talent gaps

The NFL has 32 teams drawing from one talent pool, with a draft and a salary cap built to keep them roughly
equal ([1978 and the Passing Revolution](11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) tells how the cap arrived). College
football has more than 130 teams in its top division alone, the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS), and hundreds
more below it, and no mechanism at all to keep them equal.[^fbs] Every year a few programs sign most of the
best high-school players, and everyone else has to play them.

That gap is the mother of invention. A coach who can't recruit the bigger, faster players has two choices:
lose, or change the problem. Almost every lineage in this chapter starts with a coach in the second group:
Bill Yeoman at Houston with an offensive line that couldn't block, LaVell Edwards at BYU with no chance of
out-recruiting the Southwest's powers, Hal Mumme and Mike Leach at tiny Iowa Wesleyan, Rich Rodriguez at
Glenville State, a Division II school in West Virginia. Their inventions all do the same thing in different
ways: they **change the arithmetic** so that the defense's better players have more to defend than they
have bodies, or have to make a decision they aren't trained for.

The NFL has talent gaps too, but small ones. When the other team's players are as good as yours, a gimmick
that exploits a mismatch is worth less, and a scheme that gets your quarterback hit is worth much less.

### 2. A wider field

College hash marks are 40 feet apart, 60 feet in from each sideline; NFL hash marks are 18 feet 6 inches
apart, the width of the goal posts. The field is the same size. What changes is where the ball can
start, and that changes everything about spacing. With the ball on a college hash, the short (boundary) side
is 20 yards wide and the wide (field) side 33. Before 1993 the college hashes sat even wider, a third of the
way across (53 feet 4 inches from each sideline, the high-school spot), so the wishbone and veer offenses of
this chapter played with a boundary under 18 yards wide.[^hash] [The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)
drew the same four-receiver formation on both fields.

A wide field is a gift to a **horizontal** offense, one that stretches a defense from sideline to sideline.
With 33 yards to the field side, a defense that wants to cover four receivers spread across it has to send
defenders a long way from the ball, out of the [**box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box) (the area near
the ball where runs are defended). With 20 yards to the boundary, the offense can put a single receiver into
the short side and dare a cornerback to cover him alone, with no room to help. Option and spread offenses
were made for that geometry. The NFL's narrow hashes put the ball near the middle almost every snap, which
makes the field more symmetrical and takes away some of the leverage.

### 3. Rules that tolerate the run-pass blur

College rules have been friendlier to offenses that mix run and pass on the same snap. The biggest
difference is the **ineligible downfield** rule from
[Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd#the-one-yard-rule-why-nfl-rpos-look-different):
in college an offensive lineman may be up to **three yards** past the line when a pass that crosses it is
thrown, and the rule doesn't apply at all to passes caught behind the line; in the NFL, the limit is **one
yard** on any forward pass.[^ineligible] Three yards is room to run-block for a beat and still throw. It is
the reason college RPOs can be "run first, throw later," and the reason the college game grew so many plays
that are a run and a pass at once. Other college rules nudge the same way: one foot in bounds makes a
sideline catch easier, and a defensive pass interference foul costs at most 15 yards, which changes the
math of a deep throw (the rules section near the end puts them all side by side).

### 4. Roster churn, practice limits and tempo

A college roster turns over every four or five years, and the best players leave sooner. NCAA rules cap the
hours a team can make players practice in season.[^hours] A system that has to be taught to a new quarterback
every two or three years, in limited hours, rewards **simplicity**: a small number of plays repeated until
they are automatic, which is exactly what the Air Raid and the spread option were. Simplicity, in turn, makes
**tempo** possible. A team that runs twelve concepts can call them with one word or one hand signal and snap
the ball before the defense has substituted or even lined up. College football's clock (for decades it
stopped after every first down) gave fast teams more snaps to use it on.

### The filter: what the NFL keeps

Those same four forces explain what *doesn't* cross. The NFL is a filter, and an idea has to survive four
tests to get through it.

- **The quarterback test.** NFL quarterbacks are the most expensive players in the sport, and every hit is
  a risk the team can't insure. Ideas that hit the quarterback on most snaps (the triple option, the
  wishbone) stop at the border; ideas that hit him occasionally (the zone read) cross as a change-up.
- **The talent test.** NFL defenders are fast enough, and evenly enough spread across the league, that a
  scheme built on a mismatch has to work against the *best* defense on the schedule, not the average one.
- **The rules test.** The one-yard rule, two feet in bounds and the spot-foul DPI all change how an idea
  plays on Sunday. Some ideas cross in modified form (the RPO, with quicker throws); some don't.
- **The people test.** Ideas reach the NFL most easily inside players. A quarterback who ran the zone read
  for four years arrives knowing how; a coach who designed it has to convince an NFL building to change.

The rest of the chapter follows the ideas through that filter. Here is the map.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lab-timeline
#| fig-cap: "Seventy years of borrowing: notice the long lags and how many diamonds bunch between 2012 and 2019. Each row is one college invention: the dot is roughly its college debut, the diamond when the idea became mainstream in the NFL, the label on the line the lag. Blue rows are offense, orange defense. Rows with no diamond never crossed as a system, or crossed only inside the people who learned them (BYU). Dates are approximate; several ideas, the RPO above all, have more than one claimed inventor."
ROWS = [  # idea, who, college debut, NFL arrival (None = not as a system), side, NFL note
    ("Split-T option", "Faurot, Missouri", 1941, None, "off", "never as a system"),
    ("Wing-T", "Nelson, Maine and Delaware", 1950, 2017, "off", "jet-motion era: Rams, 49ers"),
    ("Veer, triple option", "Yeoman, Houston", 1965, 2012, "off", "option reads: the 2012 wave"),
    ("Wishbone", "Bellard, Texas", 1968, None, "off", "never"),
    ("BYU passing game", "Edwards, BYU", 1972, None, "off", "carried by its QBs and coaches"),
    ("Air Raid", "Mumme and Leach", 1989, 2019, "off", "Kingsbury's Cardinals"),
    ("Zone read", "Rodriguez", 1991, 2012, "off", "Griffin, Kaepernick, Wilson"),
    ("3-3-5 stack", "Dunn, Memphis", 1991, None, "def", "college only"),
    ("Match quarters", "Saban, Michigan State", 1995, 2018, "def", "the two-high boom"),
    ("Pistol", "Ault, Nevada", 2005, 2012, "off", "Washington, 49ers"),
    ("RPO", "many claimants", 2005, 2017, "off", "Eagles, Super Bowl LII"),
    ("Up-tempo spread", "Kelly, Oregon", 2007, 2013, "off", "spread-run tempo: Kelly's Eagles"),
    ("Three-high safeties", "Heacock, Iowa State", 2017, None, "def", "college first"),
]
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.5))
n = len(ROWS)
for i, (idea, who, cy, ny, side, note) in enumerate(ROWS):
    y = n - 1 - i
    col = style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE
    ax.scatter([cy], [y], s=34, color=col, zorder=4)
    if ny is not None:
        ax.plot([cy, ny], [y, y], color=col, lw=2.2, alpha=0.45, zorder=2, solid_capstyle="round")
        ax.scatter([ny], [y], s=34, marker="D", facecolor=style.SURFACE, edgecolor=col, lw=1.6, zorder=4)
        ax.text((cy + ny) / 2, y + 0.17, f"{ny - cy} years", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center",
                va="bottom")
        ax.text(ny + 2.4, y, note, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="left")
    else:
        ax.text(cy + 2.4, y, note, fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, va="center", ha="left", style="italic")
ax.set_yticks(range(n))
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{r[0]}  ({r[1]})" for r in ROWS][::-1], fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlim(1936, 2046)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, n - 0.3)
ax.set_xticks(range(1940, 2030, 10))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.INK_2, ms=5.5, label="college debut"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="D", ls="", markerfacecolor=style.SURFACE, markeredgecolor=style.INK_2, ms=5,
            label="NFL mainstream")]
ax.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, -0.07), ncol=2, fontsize=7.2, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()

```

Two things jump out. First, the lag. Ideas that crossed took a decade or two: the zone read about twenty
years, the Air Raid thirty, the Wing-T's motion game closer to seventy. Second, the timing of the crossings
is bunched. Almost everything arrived between 2012 and 2019, as the first generation of NFL players who had
spent their whole careers in shotgun spread offenses reached the league and as NFL coaches ran out of
reasons to resist. We'll come back to why. First, the ideas, in roughly the order they were born.

## The option line: split-T, veer, wishbone, flexbone

[Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) taught how the option *works*: leave a
defender unblocked, read him, and give the ball to whoever he isn't playing. The history of that idea is a
history of college coaches finding new backfields from which to run it.

It begins in **1941** with Don Faurot at Missouri, who widened the T-formation's line splits and built the
**split-T**, a series of dives, quarterback keeps and pitches that worked like a modern option. Bud
Wilkinson took it to Oklahoma, and Oklahoma's split-T teams won 47 straight games in the 1950s
([03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#where-option-came-from-briefly) has the details). The
split-T never became an NFL offense, but it fixed the pattern for the next seventy years: option football is
what you run when the other team's linemen are bigger than yours.

**The veer (Houston, 1965).** Bill Yeoman's Houston teams of the mid-1960s couldn't block the defensive
tackles, so Yeoman stopped trying: the play-side tackle released inside and the quarterback read the first
defender outside him, giving to a diving halfback or keeping. That is the
[**veer**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-veer), and with the other halfback trailing as a pitch man it is
the [**triple option**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-triple-option). It made Houston one of the
highest-scoring teams in the country: in 1968 the Cougars beat Tulsa 100–6.[^houston]

**The wishbone (Texas, 1968).** Two years later, Texas offensive coordinator Emory Bellard moved the
split-T's fullback up close behind the quarterback and set the two halfbacks deeper and wider behind him:
the [**wishbone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wishbone) of [Classic
Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd#the-wishbone). Darrell Royal's Longhorns
won 30 straight games with it; Oklahoma and Alabama copied it; and through the 1970s it was the most feared
offense in college football.[^bellard] Here is what it was built to do.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wishbone-triple
#| fig-cap: "The wishbone triple option to the split-end side (the offense's left). Notice that every play-side defender is either blocked or read. The left tackle releases inside to the Mike, leaving the 5-technique unblocked as the dive key (#1); the Will, on the line outside him, is the pitch key (#2). The fullback (F) dives; the near halfback arcs around #2 to block the safety in the alley (#3); the split end (X) blocks the cornerback (#4). The far halfback sprints behind the quarterback to become the pitch man, about four yards outside him and a yard deeper, so #2 can't cover both. The quarterback rides the dive reading #1, then, if he keeps, runs at #2."
def wishbone_off():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -3.6, 0.0, "F"),
                     O("LH", "RB", -5.2, -2.6, "H"), O("RH", "RB", -5.2, 2.6, "H"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X")]
    check_legal(off)
    return off


def wishbone_def():
    return [D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "2i"),
            D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 1.0, -7.8, "W"), D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -0.8, "M"),
            D("SS", "SS", 7.5, -10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 1.5, "FS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 10.0, "CB")]


p = Play(wishbone_off(), wishbone_def(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LT", (3.4, -1.3), via=[(0.0, -2.9)])           # veer release to the Mike
go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -1.1))                               # on the 2i
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, 0.5))                                 # back on the 1
go_to(p, "RG", (2.8, 1.6), via=[(0.2, 1.7)])              # climb for backside pursuit
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 3.7))
go_to(p, "Y", (0.6, 5.7))
go_to(p, "LH", (6.3, -10.0), via=[(-3.6, -6.4), (-0.6, -10.2)])   # arc around #2 to #3
go_to(p, "X", (5.4, -14.8))
go_to(p, "RH", (-2.8, -10.2), "path", via=[(-5.6, 0.4), (-4.6, -6.0)])   # the pitch man: 4 wide, 1 deep
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 11.5), window=(-6.8, 15.2), title=False, width_in=6.4)
read_line(f, p, (-2.4, -1.2), (1.0, -4.0))
read_line(f, p, (-2.4, -1.2), (1.0, -7.8))
branch(f, p, [(-3.6, 0.0), (-2.4, -1.6), (4.6, -2.4)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="dive",
       label_at=(6.5, -2.7), fontsize=7)
branch(f, p, [(-2.4, -1.2), (-1.5, -5.2), (-0.4, -6.4), (5.2, -6.6)], color=GREEN, label="keep",
       label_at=(6.5, -6.6), fontsize=7)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-1.6, -5.4), (-2.8, -9.6))
branch(f, p, [(-2.8, -10.2), (-0.6, -11.6), (4.6, -12.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="pitch",
       label_at=(2.4, -14.0), fontsize=7)
for num, (d, w) in {"1": (2.8, -4.2), "2": (2.8, -8.0), "3": (9.5, -10.0), "4": (8.4, -15.2)}.items():
    say(f, p, d, w, num, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=8.5, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 11.9, -5.6, "1 = dive key (first read)\n2 = pitch key (second read)\n3 = alley: the lead halfback\n"
    "4 = deep: the split end", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, 6.6), (-5.4, 2.0), "pitch man starts\non the far side", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-5.4, -13.8), (-3.4, -6.6), "lead halfback arcs\naround #2 to #3", fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(f.ax, "The wishbone triple option", size=10)
plt.show()
```

The wishbone's genius was that **every back had a job on every play, to either side**: dive, lead or pitch.
The defense had to assign someone to each of three runners on both sides of the formation, with every
assignment perfect, and do it without knowing which way the play was going until the snap. In 1971
Oklahoma's wishbone averaged 472.4 rushing yards a game, still the major-college record.[^ou71]

Why did it fade? The same forces that made it, in reverse. **Defenses got faster** through the 1970s and
1980s, and fast defenders who play their assignments shrink the margins the triple option lives on. **The
best high-school quarterbacks wanted to pass**, because passers were what the NFL drafted, and the
programs that could recruit them stopped needing a talent equalizer. And **it was hard to come from behind
with** an offense that threw a dozen times a game. Oklahoma won its last national title with the wishbone in
1985; by the 1990s the formation survived mostly at the service academies (Army, Navy and Air Force).[^bonedecline]

**The flexbone (late 1970s and 1980s).** The wishbone's last descendant fixed its biggest weakness, width.
By standing the two halfbacks just off the line as slotbacks (A-backs), the
[**flexbone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flexbone) spread the defense like a passing formation while
keeping three runners near the ball; one A-back's pre-snap motion became the pitch. Its invention is
disputed. The name is usually traced to Fisher DeBerry's Air Force teams of the 1980s (the wishbone, he is
said to have remarked, needed to be more flexible), and Ken Hatfield, DeBerry's predecessor there, ran a
version at Arkansas later in the decade. Paul Johnson, Georgia Southern's offensive coordinator from 1985, is
the coach most credited with building it into a full system, and the formation itself is the double-slot set
of the run-and-shoot (more on that offense below) with the option added. Johnson's Navy and Georgia Tech teams are its modern face
([02-03](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd#the-flexbone)).[^flexbone]

Put the four option backfields side by side and the idea's survival strategy is plain: the *three threats*
never change; only where the threats start does.

```{python}
#| label: fig-triple-backfields
#| fig-cap: "One idea, four backfields: the three threats never change, only where they start. Offense only, plus the two read keys (#1 dive key, #2 pitch key), option to the offense's left. In the three under-center panels the inside runner (thick dark arrow) hits just inside #1, the quarterback (green) keeps outside him, and the pitch man (thin arrow, brown arc) stays outside #2, about four yards wide and a yard deeper than the quarterback: in the veer the backside halfback, in the wishbone the far halfback, in the flexbone the backside A-back in motion. In the spread option the give goes the other way, away from the read, and the third threat is a throw: a bubble screen to the slot. The pitch has become a pass."
def keys():
    return [D("K1", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "1"), D("K2", "OLB", 1.0, -7.8, "2")]


def bf_split():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("LH", "RB", -4.6, -2.2, "H"), O("RH", "RB", -4.6, 2.2, "H")]
    return off, [((-4.6, -2.2), [(-3.0, -2.4), (2.6, -2.7)], "run"),
                 ((-4.6, 2.2), [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.2, -5.6), (-2.6, -9.6)], "path")], (-2.5, -1.3)


def bf_bone():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -3.6, 0.0, "F"),
                     O("LH", "RB", -5.2, -2.6, "H"), O("RH", "RB", -5.2, 2.6, "H")]
    return off, [((-3.6, 0.0), [(-2.4, -1.6), (2.6, -2.5)], "run"),
                 ((-5.2, 2.6), [(-5.6, 0.2), (-4.4, -5.8), (-2.8, -9.8)], "path"),
                 ((-5.2, -2.6), [(-3.4, -6.2), (-0.6, -10.4), (3.2, -10.6)], "path")], (-2.4, -1.2)


def bf_flex():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0.0, "B"),
                     O("LA", "RB", -1.6, -5.2, "A"), O("RA", "RB", -1.6, 5.2, "A")]
    return off, [((-4.6, 0.0), [(-2.6, -1.6), (2.6, -2.5)], "run"),
                 ((-1.6, 5.2), [(-3.6, 1.6), (-4.4, -2.0), (-3.8, -6.4), (-2.6, -9.6)], "path"),
                 ((-1.6, -5.2), [(-0.8, -8.6), (0.4, -10.6), (3.2, -10.6)], "path")], (-2.4, -1.2)


def bf_spread():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.6, "R"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H")]
    return off, [((-5.0, -2.6), [(-3.8, 0.7), (2.6, 1.8)], "run"),
                 ((-1.5, -9.0), [(-2.9, -10.2), (-2.8, -12.8)], "path")], (-5.0, 0.0)


PANELS = [("Split-back veer (Houston, 1965)", bf_split, (-1.6, -5.0), (-2.7, -9.0)),
          ("Wishbone (Texas, 1968)", bf_bone, (-1.6, -5.2), (-2.9, -9.2)),
          ("Flexbone (1980s)", bf_flex, (-0.9, -4.4), (-2.8, -9.2)),
          ("Spread option (2000s)", bf_spread, (-2.4, -4.2), (-2.8, -12.0))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5.0))
for ax, (title, fn, toss_from, toss_to) in zip(axes.flat, PANELS):
    off, paths, mesh = fn()
    dfn = keys() if fn is not bf_spread else [D("K1", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "1"), D("K2", "NB", 3.0, -6.8, "2")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-14.6, 7.2), window=(-6.6, 4.8), title=False)
    for start, pts, kind in paths:
        full = [start] + pts
        if kind == "run":
            branch(f, p, full, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.2, dash="-")
        else:
            branch(f, p, full, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4, dash="-")
    qb = p.players["QB"]
    if fn is bf_spread:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.4, -1.4), (-2.6, -4.4), (0.4, -6.0), (3.4, -6.2)], color=GREEN, lw=1.8)
    else:
        branch(f, p, [(qb.d, 0.0), mesh, (-1.0, -4.2), (0.6, -6.0), (3.4, -6.2)], color=GREEN, lw=1.8)
    pitch_arc(f, p, toss_from, toss_to)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

What crossed into the NFL from this line was never a formation. It was the **idea** in the last panel: a
quarterback who reads one defender instead of blocking him, run from the shotgun, with a third threat that
can be a throw. That idea needed thirty more years and two more inventions, the spread offense and the zone
read, before it could reach Sunday.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Oklahoma 1971"}
The 1971 Sooners, coached by Chuck Fairbanks with Barry Switzer as offensive coordinator, are the wishbone
at its peak: quarterback Jack Mildren, halfback Greg Pruitt and the 472-yard rushing average. Their most
famous game is the one they lost, 35–31 to Nebraska in Norman on Thanksgiving Day, the "Game of the
Century" between the top two teams in the country.[^gotc]

**What to notice** on the replays that circulate online: count the defenders Nebraska puts on each side of
the ball, and watch how often a Nebraska defender who did his one job perfectly still ended up tackling a man
without the ball. Then watch the pitch man's spacing on the long runs: four or five yards outside the
quarterback and a yard deeper, so the pitch key can never take both.
:::

## The Wing-T and BYU: misdirection and the passing equalizer

Not every college lineage was an option. Two others, one running and one passing, fed the NFL more
quietly.

**The Wing-T (Maine and Delaware, about 1950).** Dave Nelson crossed the T-formation with the single wing's
wingback to make the [**Wing-T**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wing-t), and his successor at Delaware,
Tubby Raymond, ran it for 36 seasons.[^wingt] Its logic, taught in [Perimeter Runs and
Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd#the-wing-t-an-order-of-football), is
**series football**: several plays that start with the same backfield action and end differently, so a
defense that flows to the first thing it sees is punished. The
[buck sweep](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-buck-sweep), the trap, the counter and the waggle (the
quarterback fakes the sweep and rolls out the other way to pass) all start the same way. The Wing-T itself
never became an NFL offense, but its *logic* did, twice: through high-school coaches such as Gus Malzahn, who
ran its series from the shotgun at Auburn (below), and through the NFL's jet-motion era of the late 2010s.
Sean McVay's Rams and Kyle Shanahan's 49ers ran what is, in effect, a Wing-T series with a receiver in the wingback's
role: the jet sweep one way, then the same motion with a handoff the other way, then the same motion with
a bootleg pass off it. The defense that flows to the motion is punished, which is the Wing-T's whole
idea ([03-05](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) has the film rooms). That is why the
timeline gives the Wing-T an NFL diamond in 2017, while admitting it is the idea, not the formation, that
crossed.

**BYU (1972 to 2000).** LaVell Edwards took over a Brigham Young program in Provo, Utah, that had no hope of
out-recruiting the big programs, and decided to throw. Through the 1970s and 1980s BYU passed when almost
nobody else in college football did, spreading the ball to backs and tight ends with timing routes and
crossing patterns, and produced a line of record-setting quarterbacks: Gifford Nielsen, Marc Wilson, Jim
McMahon, Steve Young, Robbie Bosco and Ty Detmer, who won the Heisman Trophy in 1990. In 1984 BYU went 13–0 and
won the national title.[^byu]

BYU's passing game didn't cross into the NFL as a system. It crossed in **people**, which is the first
example of a pattern this chapter keeps finding. McMahon won a Super Bowl with the 1985 Bears and Young two
MVP awards with the 49ers; Mike Holmgren, BYU's quarterbacks coach in the early 1980s, went to San Francisco
and later built the Packers' West Coast offense; Andy Reid played offensive line for Edwards; and Norm Chow,
Edwards's assistant for 27 years and his play-caller from 1982, became one of college football's most
celebrated offensive coordinators at USC and, briefly, the Tennessee Titans'.[^byupeople] And BYU's spacing and
crossing routes became the raw material of the next lineage.

**The run-and-shoot (Portland State, 1975 to 1980).** The NFL side of this offense is in
[11-02](11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd); its roots are a textbook small-school story. Glenn "Tiger" Ellison
designed it as a high-school coach in Middletown, Ohio, and Mouse Davis, after 15 seasons coaching high
school in Oregon, refined it as Portland State's head coach, where June Jones and then Neil Lomax set
passing records. Davis carried it to the USFL's Houston Gamblers in 1984 and the
Detroit Lions in 1988.[^mouse]

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Every lineage so far answers the same problem: **the other team has better players.** The option answers it
by reading a defender instead of blocking him (one fewer man to beat), the Wing-T by making the defense guess
wrong about where the ball is going (defenders who flow the wrong way don't count), and BYU's passing game by
spreading the ball to five receivers so a bigger, slower defense has to cover all of them. Each trade is
real. The option gives up the passing game and puts the quarterback in harm's way; the Wing-T gives up width
and demands huge practice time for its fakes; the passing game gives up the clock (every incompletion stops
it, so a passing team can't sit on a lead) and asks a quarterback to be very good. College coaches could make those trades because their alternative was losing. NFL coaches,
whose players are evenly matched, usually take the idea and leave the trade.
:::

## The Air Raid: subtraction as a strategy

Hal Mumme was the head coach at Iowa Wesleyan, an NAIA school (a small-college association outside the
NCAA's divisions) in Mount Pleasant, Iowa, when he hired a
law-school graduate turned coach named Mike Leach as his offensive coordinator in 1989. Their plan, borrowed openly from
BYU and then pushed much further, was to throw on almost every down from four- and five-receiver sets, with
very wide line splits, and to run **very few plays** practised an enormous number of times. Leach gave it
its name, helped by an old air-raid siren that a fan sounded after touchdowns (accounts differ on whether
that began at Iowa Wesleyan or at their next stop). The pair took it to
Valdosta State (1992–1996) and then to Kentucky, where in 1998 quarterback Tim Couch became a consensus
All-American and, the next spring, the first pick in the NFL draft.[^airraid]

[Offensive Systems](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd#the-air-raid-a-few-plays-a-thousand-reps)
explains the Air Raid's *language* (one-word calls, a slim playbook) and
[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) draws its signature concepts:
[mesh](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mesh), the [shallow cross](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd#shallow-cross-the-air-raids-bread-and-butter),
[Y-cross](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-y-cross) and
[four verticals](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-verticals). What matters for this chapter is
**why a small menu was a weapon**:

- **Repetition beats variety** when your players are worse. A quarterback who has read the same mesh concept
  against every coverage ten thousand times throws it before the defender has finished deciding.
- **A small menu travels.** It can be taught quickly to a new quarterback every two or three years, and it
  fits on a wristband or in a hand signal, which makes the no-huddle easy.
- **Spreading five receivers shrinks the box**, so even a pass-first team can run the ball against a light
  front (more on that arithmetic in the next section).

Leach became Texas Tech's head coach in 2000 and spent a decade there, then Washington State and Mississippi
State, until his death in December 2022. His tree became the Air Raid's distribution network: Dana
Holgorsen, Sonny Dykes, Kliff Kingsbury and Lincoln Riley among many others.[^leachtree] Riley's Oklahoma
and USC offenses produced three Heisman-winning quarterbacks who went first in the NFL draft: Baker Mayfield
(2017 Heisman), Kyler Murray (2018) and Caleb Williams (2022).[^riley]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Texas Tech vs. Texas, November 1, 2008"}
Leach's best team, quarterback Graham Harrell and receiver Michael Crabtree, beat top-ranked Texas 39–33 in
Lubbock when Crabtree caught a pass near the sideline, kept his feet and scored with one second left.[^tt2008]

**What to notice:** count the plays. Texas Tech's offense ran a handful of concepts all night from
spread formations with very wide line splits. Wide splits widen the gaps between the defensive linemen too,
which makes stunts harder to run, forces the defense to show where its pressure is coming from, and opens
clear throwing windows for a quarterback on a quick three- or five-step drop. And watch where the ball went:
short and quick to the sideline, again and again, to receivers who caught it and ran, until the defense
crept up and the vertical route behind them came open.
:::

The Air Raid's route into the NFL ran through its quarterbacks and coaches. Patrick Mahomes played for
Kingsbury at Texas Tech;
Kingsbury became the Cardinals' head coach in 2019, hired straight from college with no NFL coaching
experience to bring the Air Raid with him,[^kingsbury] and later Washington's offensive coordinator with Jayden Daniels (04-08 has that film room). Mesh, the shallow
cross and four verticals are now in every NFL playbook. What the NFL left at the border was the *pure*
system: the very wide line splits that NFL pass rushers would knife through, the near-total absence of a
power run game, and the refusal to go under center.

## The spread offense: a philosophy, not a formation

By the late 1990s these lineages were converging on one idea, and it's worth naming exactly, because the
word gets used loosely. A [**spread offense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spread-offense) lines up in
the shotgun with three or four receivers spread across the field so that the defense must send defenders
out of the box to cover them, then attacks the space that leaves, with quick passes, with option reads, or
with both. [Spread and Modern Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd#formation-not-philosophy)
drew the distinction: a *spread formation* is a picture every NFL team uses; a *spread offense* is the whole
system built on that picture.

The core of the philosophy is arithmetic, the [hat math](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) of
the run game (count blockers against defenders; the side with more wins) applied to the whole field.

```{python}
#| label: fig-spread-math
#| fig-cap: "Why spread out to run? Count the shaded box in each panel. Left, a 1970s-style I-formation (21 personnel; FB the fullback) against a 4-3 with the strong safety down: eight in the box against seven blockers, and the quarterback, who just hands off, blocks nobody, so one defender is always free. Right, a four-receiver spread (10 personnel) against nickel: the receivers have pulled five defenders wide, two of them apex defenders (NB and SS, ringed) halfway between the box and the slots. Six in the box against five linemen, and the quarterback's read makes it six against six. If an apex defender steps in to make it seven, the slot outside him is uncovered. (Wide receivers and cornerbacks are outside both pictures.)"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 4.6))
# left: I-formation vs 8-man box
off_i = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "FB"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                   O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
check_legal(off_i)
dfn_i = [D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("7", 1), "7"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
         D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
         D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
         D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 3.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS"),
         D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off_i, dfn_i, los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-8.6, 14.0), title=False)
box_shade(f, p, -0.2, 7.2, -6.2, 8.4)
say(f, p, 9.4, -9.0, "8 in the box\nv 7 blockers", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -5.0, -6.6, "Q hands off:\nblocks nobody", fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(axes[0], "1970s: I-formation v eight in the box", size=8.6)
# right: spread vs nickel
dfn_s = [D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -1), "3"),
         D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"), D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
         D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.0, "M"),
         D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.6, "NB"), D("SS", "SS", 4.5, 6.6, "SS"),
         D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread10(), dfn_s, los=35, to_go=None)
check_legal(spread10())
p.highlight("NB", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-8.6, 14.0), title=False)
box_shade(f, p, -0.2, 7.2, -4.6, 4.6)
say(f, p, 9.4, -9.0, "6 in the box\nv 5 blockers\n+ the QB's read", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -5.4, 7.6, "apex defenders:\nbox or slot?", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(axes[1], "2000s: four wide v six in the box", size=8.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

That is the whole idea in one picture. **Spreading out is a way to run the ball**, not only a way to throw
it: four receivers take five defenders out of the box, and a defense that brings one back in leaves a
receiver alone. The spread then needs one more thing to finish the job, because six defenders against five
blockers is still one free man. Two answers emerged, and they split the spread into two families:

- **Spread to pass** (the Air Raid, and Joe Tiller's Purdue offense with Drew Brees, which Tiller himself
  called "basketball on grass"):[^tiller] accept the free man and throw quickly to whoever the defense left
  alone.
- **Spread to run** (Rich Rodriguez, Urban Meyer and their heirs): make the quarterback a runner, so the
  read takes care of the free man. That is the spread option, next.

The NFL already had plenty of the first family: the run-and-shoot, the K-Gun and, later, the 2007 Patriots
spread out to throw without help from Saturday. What it imported from college was mostly the second, the
spread *run* game, as the shotgun data near the end of the chapter shows.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The spread is a passing offense." Some spread offenses are, but the most influential ones were run-first.
Rich Rodriguez's West Virginia, Urban Meyer's Florida and Gus Malzahn's Auburn won with the run game, using
the spread to empty the box and the quarterback's legs to win the numbers. The NFL data later in the chapter
makes the same point: the shotgun crossed into the NFL first on passing downs, and only later, as the spread
run game came with it, on running plays.
:::

## The spread option: Rodriguez, Meyer and the quarterback's legs

The [**spread option**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spread-option) is a spread offense whose run game is
built on option reads from the shotgun. Its origin story is one of the best in football, and
[03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#where-option-came-from-briefly) tells it: at Glenville
State in 1991, Rich Rodriguez's quarterback fumbled a zone-play handoff in practice, picked the ball up, saw
the backside end crashing down on the running back, and ran where the end had been.[^rr] Rodriguez saw the
mistake was a play. The [zone read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-read) married the option's read
to the most common run in football, inside zone, and to the shotgun, where the quarterback could see the
read key and the receivers at once.

Rodriguez took it to Tulane and Clemson as an offensive coordinator, then to West Virginia as head coach
(2001–2007), where quarterback Pat White and running back Steve Slaton made it the most dangerous running
offense in the country. Urban Meyer, at Bowling Green, Utah and Florida, built his own spread option on the
same principles, with bigger quarterbacks who could run between the tackles: Alex Smith, whose unbeaten 2004
Utah team won the Fiesta Bowl before Smith went first in the 2005 draft, and Tim Tebow, the 2007 Heisman
winner, whose Florida teams won national titles in the 2006 and 2008 seasons.[^meyer]

What made the spread option more than the zone read was what Rodriguez *attached* to it. With four receivers
spread out, the defense's apex defenders (the ones ringed in @fig-spread-math) are stuck between the box and
the slots. Rodriguez's quarterbacks read **two** defenders on the same side: the end, to give or keep, and
then the apex defender, to keep or throw a bubble screen to the slot. It is the triple option's logic with
the pitch replaced by a pass.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rodriguez
#| fig-cap: "The spread option's three-way play, as Rodriguez's West Virginia teams ran it: the zone read with a bubble screen attached. The line zones to the right and leaves the left end (ringed) unblocked; the quarterback reads him first (dashed green line). If the end stays wide, the quarterback gives (dark dashed arrow) and the back runs the inside-zone track. If the end crashes, the quarterback pulls the ball and reads the second defender on that side, the apex nickel back (ringed), who has to choose between the quarterback and the slot receiver. If the nickel comes up to take the quarterback, the quarterback throws the bubble (brown arc) to H, with X blocking the cornerback; if the nickel widens with H, the quarterback keeps (green dashed arrow) into the space the end and the nickel left. Two reads, three possible ball carriers: the triple option from the shotgun, with a pass as the third option."
def zrb_defense():
    return [D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -1), "3"),
            D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"), D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.0, "M"),
            D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -7.0, "NB"), D("SS", "SS", 4.5, 7.0, "SS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS")]


p = Play(spread10(), zrb_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LT", (0.45, -2.75), via=[(-0.3, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "LG", (3.0, -1.6), via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (0.6, -1.5)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.45))
go_to(p, "RG", (3.1, 2.0), via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.7, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.55, 3.75))
go_to(p, "X", (5.0, -15.8))
go_to(p, "H", (-2.2, -14.8), "route", via=[(-3.0, -10.6)])        # the bubble: bow back, then widen
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("NB", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.6, 9.6), window=(-7.6, 11.0), title=False, width_in=6.4)
# the two reads, numbered in order
read_line(f, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (1.0, -4.3), num="1", at=0.45)
read_line(f, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (4.5, -7.0), num="2", at=0.78)
# give: the back starts from his own spot, crosses in front of the quarterback (the mesh) and runs inside zone
branch(f, p, [(-5.4, -2.4), (-3.8, -0.4), (-2.4, 1.1), (0.6, 1.2), (4.6, 0.5)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="give if the\nend stays", label_at=(7.6, 0.6), fontsize=6.8)
# keep: the quarterback pulls and runs outside the crashing end, inside the widening nickel
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.2, -2.2), (-2.4, -4.9), (0.4, -6.0), (3.2, -5.6), (6.8, -4.6)], color=GREEN,
       label="keep if the\nnickel widens", label_at=(8.8, -6.6), fontsize=6.8)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-4.3, -2.0), (-2.5, -13.4), rad=0.16)
say(f, p, -5.8, -13.4, "throw the bubble if\nthe nickel takes Q", color=style.BALL, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-6.4, 3.6), (-4.4, -1.3), "mesh: Q rides the\nball in R's belly", fontsize=6.4, shrink=2)
point_to(f, p, (8.0, -12.6), (4.6, -7.2), "read 2: the\napex nickel", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (2.6, -12.4), (0.7, -4.6), "read 1:\nthe end", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(f.ax, "Zone read with the bubble attached", size=10)
plt.show()
```

Here are the two branches that come out after the end crashes, in motion.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rodriguez-anim
#| fig-cap: "The zone read with the bubble attached, two branches after the end crashes (simulated, BDB-format tracking; orange rings mark the two read defenders, the green ring follows the ball; only the left side of the field is shown). Watch the nickel in frame 2: he decides the play. Top row: he widens with the bubble, so the quarterback keeps into the space both defenders left. Bottom row: he steps up at the quarterback, so the ball goes out to H behind X's block. Two defenders on that side, three threats."
def zrb_play(nickel_widens):
    p = Play(spread10(), zrb_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
    # defense first (blocks aim at where they end up)
    go_to(p, "BT", (1.3, -2.0), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "PT", (1.4, 0.9), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "PE", (1.4, 4.4), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.4, -0.6), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 2.6), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "BE", (-1.2, -2.2), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.15)          # the crash
    go_to(p, "BE", (-1.6, -0.6), "path", speed=2.5)
    go_to(p, "LCB", (5.0, -15.6), "path", speed=1.5, delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "FS", (10.5, -3.0), "path", speed=2.5, delay=0.4)
    if nickel_widens:
        go_to(p, "NB", (1.0, -12.2), "path", speed=5.5, delay=0.2)
    else:
        go_to(p, "NB", (-1.8, -5.0), "path", speed=4.6, delay=0.2)
    # offense: inside zone right
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.45, -2.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.2, -1.0), speed=2.6, via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (0.6, -1.5)])
    go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.45), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RG", (2.3, 2.1), speed=2.6, via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.7, 2.0)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.55, 3.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "X", (4.0, -15.6), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "H", (-2.4, -12.2), "route", via=[(-2.9, -10.4)], speed=5.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.9, 0.7), "run", speed=3.5, delay=0.25, via=[(-4.3, -0.4)])   # the mesh (a fake)
    go_to(p, "RB", (2.6, 2.6), "path", speed=6.0, via=[(-1.2, 2.3)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.2, 0.0), "path", speed=0.5)
    if nickel_widens:
        go_to(p, "QB", (6.0, -6.8), "run", speed=6.8, delay=0.2, via=[(-4.9, -1.0), (-3.6, -3.6), (-1.0, -5.8)])
        go_to(p, "H", (-1.4, -13.2), "path", speed=3.0)
    else:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, -3.8), "run", speed=5.5, delay=0.2, via=[(-4.9, -1.0)])
        p.pass_to("H", t=1.45)
        go_to(p, "H", (5.0, -11.6), "run", speed=6.5, delay=0.15, via=[(-1.8, -12.4)])
    return p


TIMES_ZRB = [0.9, 1.45, 2.2]
NOTES_ZRB = ["End crashes on R:\nQ pulls the ball", "Nickel widens with H:\nQ keeps", "Q runs where the end\nand the nickel were",
             "End crashes on R:\nQ pulls the ball", "Nickel steps up at Q:\nthe ball goes out", "H runs behind\nX's block"]
option_animation([zrb_play(True), zrb_play(False)], TIMES_ZRB, lateral=(-17.6, 3.0), window=(-7.0, 7.0),
                 notes=NOTES_ZRB, rows=["Nickel widens: keep", "Nickel attacks: throw"],
                 rings=(("BE", style.DEFENSE), ("NB", style.DEFENSE)))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: West Virginia, Sugar Bowl, January 2, 2006"}
Rodriguez's West Virginia, with a freshman quarterback, Pat White, and a freshman running back, Steve
Slaton, beat Georgia 38–35 in the Sugar Bowl, played that year in Atlanta while New Orleans recovered from
Hurricane Katrina. Slaton ran for 204 yards, a Sugar Bowl record.[^sugar]

**What to notice:** on the zone reads, find the backside end first, then the apex defender over the slot.
Georgia's defense, built to beat the power-running SEC, had fast, big defenders, and it still spent the night
a step late, because every snap asked two of them to make a decision they usually didn't get to practise.
:::

## Pistol, tempo and the RPO: the 2000s laboratory

Three more inventions finished the modern college offense, and each one came from a coach looking for an
edge the others didn't have.

**The pistol (Nevada, 2005).** Chris Ault put his quarterback about four yards behind the center, between
under-center and shotgun depth, with the running back directly behind him. The
[pistol](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pistol) ([02-02](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd#pistol))
kept the shotgun's view for the quarterback's read while letting the back run downhill to either side, so
the defense couldn't tell the play's direction from his alignment. In 2009 Nevada had three 1,000-yard
rushers, one of them the quarterback, Colin Kaepernick.[^ault]

**Tempo (Oregon, Auburn and many others).** Chip Kelly, Oregon's offensive coordinator from 2007 and head
coach from 2009 to 2012, ran the spread option at a pace college football had never seen: plays signalled
from the sideline with picture boards (big posters whose pictures code the play), the ball snapped as soon as
the officials allowed. Kelly went 46–7 as
Oregon's head coach.[^kelly] Gus Malzahn, a former Arkansas high-school coach who had learned offense from
the Delaware Wing-T book, combined tempo, the shotgun and Wing-T misdirection; as Auburn's offensive
coordinator he won the 2010 national title with quarterback Cam Newton (the play we now call the
[inverted veer](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-inverted-veer) was one of their signatures), and as head
coach he won the 2013 Iron Bowl on the "Kick Six."[^malzahn] [In-Game Adjustments and
Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd) explains what tempo does to a defense:
it freezes the defense's personnel and its calls, and wears it down.

Why did tempo work so much better on Saturday? Partly the clock, which (as the first section said) stopped
after every first down until 2023, handing a fast team even more snaps. Partly the roster: a college team's backups are much
weaker than its starters, so a defense that can't substitute, or has to play its second string because the
first is exhausted, loses more than an NFL defense would. And partly the menu: tempo needs the small,
signal-sized playbook the spread already had.

Defenses fought back with the only tool they had left, the rulebook. In October 2012 Nick Saban, whose
Alabama defenses were built to substitute by situation, complained about no-huddle offenses and asked, "Is
this what we want football to be?"[^saban2012] In 2014 the NCAA's rules committee proposed making offenses
wait until 10 seconds had run off the play clock before snapping, so defenses could substitute; after an
outcry from coaches, the proposal was tabled before it could be voted on.[^tensec] The offense had won the
argument. The best evidence came from the critic himself. Saban's Alabama, the most
dominant defensive program of the 2010s, lost games to up-tempo spread teams (including Malzahn's Auburn on
the Kick Six and Ohio State's spread offense in the playoff that ended the 2014 season), and Saban answered
by hiring offensive coordinators who brought spread and up-tempo ideas, starting with Lane Kiffin in 2014. By
2020 his national champions were an up-tempo, RPO-heavy spread offense that set a school scoring
record.[^saban]

**The RPO (everyone, 2000s–2010s).** Put a quick throw on a running play and you have the
[RPO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rpo). [Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd#where-rpos-came-from)
tells its tangled origin story (Air Raid tags, Rodriguez's bubbles, Meyer's accidental discovery at Utah,
Brett Favre's claim to have done it on his own) and why no single inventor can be named. The laboratory
conditions explain why it was college that made it routine: the three-yard rule from the first section let
linemen run-block while the quarterback decided, and a bubble or now screen thrown behind the line wasn't
covered by it at all. Art Briles's Baylor teams took the RPO to an
extreme, with receivers split almost to the sideline and the quarterback, Robert Griffin III in 2011, reading
defenders on the run and the throw on the same snap.[^briles]

## The defense strikes back

Every offensive idea in this chapter created a problem for defenses, and college defenses, facing a spread
offense almost every week, solved those problems first. Four answers matter.

### The 3-3-5 stack: speed and mystery

The first answer was simply to match the offense's speed with defensive backs.
The [**3-3-5 stack**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-3-5-stack) has three down linemen, three linebackers
stacked directly behind them, and five defensive backs, two of whom are hybrids, safeties who play like
linebackers, aligned outside the box over the slots. Joe Lee Dunn is usually credited with its first modern
version, at Memphis in 1991, born of the familiar college reason: he didn't have enough big defensive linemen,
so he swapped one for a defensive back.[^stack] (Be careful with the name.
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd#three-meanings)
explains that NFL coaches use "[3-3-5](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-3-5)" for something else: a
five-man line in nickel, not this stack.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-335-stack
#| fig-cap: "The 3-3-5 stack against a four-receiver spread: same picture, different five rushers. Both panels start from one alignment: three down linemen (a nose and two 5-techniques), three linebackers stacked behind them, and two hybrid safeties (SP, the spur, and BA, the bandit) over the slots, with the cornerbacks out of the picture and one deep free safety. Eight defenders could rush, but only three have a hand down. Left: the line slants right while the Mike and Will blitz through the gaps it vacated. Right: the line slants left, the Sam and the bandit come from the right, and the Mike rotates toward the pressure to wall off the slot, with the Will in the middle and the spur to the weak side: three under, three deep. A protection set for the first picture is wrong for the second."
def stack_def():
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, technique("5", -1), "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 0.0, "M"),
            D("SAM", "SAM", 4.6, technique("5", 1), "S"),
            D("SP", "DB", 5.0, -7.2, "SP"), D("BA", "DB", 5.0, 7.2, "BA"),
            D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB")]


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 4.2))
for ax, version in zip(axes, ("A", "B")):
    p = Play(spread10(), stack_def(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if version == "A":
        go_to(p, "LE", (-1.2, -2.4), "rush", speed=4.0)           # slant inside, through the B gap
        go_to(p, "N", (-0.8, 1.0), "rush", speed=4.0)             # slant to the right A gap
        go_to(p, "RE", (-1.2, 4.6), "rush", speed=4.0)            # contain rush
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (-1.9, -0.8), "rush", speed=5.0, via=[(1.0, -0.6)])   # left A gap
        go_to(p, "WILL", (-2.0, -4.4), "rush", speed=5.0, via=[(1.0, -4.3)])   # left C gap
        go_to(p, "SAM", (8.6, 3.6), "path", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "SP", (8.2, -6.6), "path", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "BA", (8.6, 8.6), "path", speed=4.0)
        p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
        title = "Pressure 1: Mike and Will"
    else:
        go_to(p, "LE", (-1.2, -4.8), "rush", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "N", (-0.8, -1.0), "rush", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "RE", (-1.2, 2.4), "rush", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "SAM", (-1.9, 4.0), "rush", speed=5.0, via=[(1.0, 4.4)])
        go_to(p, "BA", (-2.0, 5.6), "rush", speed=5.5, via=[(1.2, 6.8)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (7.5, 5.5), "path", speed=4.0)          # rotates to the pressure side: walls F
        go_to(p, "WILL", (7.8, -1.0), "path", speed=4.0)         # the middle hook
        go_to(p, "SP", (8.0, -8.5), "path", speed=4.0)           # weak curl/flat
        p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("BA", color=style.DEFENSE)
        title = "Pressure 2: Sam and bandit"
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-6.8, 14.4), title=False)
    panel_title(ax, title, size=8.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The stack's weapons are **speed** (an extra defensive back against an extra receiver) and **mystery**:
with eight potential rushers and only three hands in the dirt, a protection scheme that counts the
defenders on the line before the snap counts only three. (The hybrid safeties' names are a dialect:
*spur* and *bandit* are West Virginia's words; other staffs say *star*, *rover*, *viper*, or simply strong
and weak safety, so expect a broadcast to use any of them.) Its price is size. Three linemen against five offensive linemen can be
pushed around, which is why the stack thrived in conferences full of spread passing offenses and struggled
against teams that lined up with tight ends and ran straight at it: double-team a down lineman, climb to a
stacked linebacker who has no one in front of him, and the light front has nothing left. West Virginia, under Rodriguez's
defensive coordinator Jeff Casteel, paired the stack with the spread option, so the Mountaineers practised
against the offense they defended.[^casteel]
The NFL never adopted it as a base defense; NFL offensive lines are too good to give away a lineman every
down.

### Quarters and pattern matching: the college two-high

The second answer was in the secondary. Against spread offenses that ran option and play-action from the same
looks on wide college hashes, a defense that put a safety in the box got beaten deep, and one that kept
two safeties deep got run over. [**Quarters**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarters) with
[pattern matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pattern-matching) let it do both: two safeties 10 to 12
yards deep who read the receivers in front of them, carry the vertical routes and fit the run from depth
when it shows. [Quarters and Match Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd#a-short-history-from-cleveland-to-east-lansing-and-iowa-city)
tells this history in full: Nick Saban's pattern-match rules, developed as Bill Belichick's coordinator in
Cleveland and refined at Michigan State, LSU and Alabama; Mark Dantonio and Pat Narduzzi's Michigan State;
Iowa's long-running split-field quarters; Gary Patterson's
[4-2-5](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4-2-5) at TCU.

This is the one lineage that made a round trip. Its roots were in an NFL building (Cleveland in the early
1990s), it matured on college fields against the spread, and when NFL offenses went spread in the late 2010s,
NFL defenses went back to the college quarters coaches for the answer. NFL Next Gen Stats measured
split-safety coverage on 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018 and 42.0% in 2025, the highest since tracking began.[^ngs]

### Tite and mint: walling off the middle

The third answer was a front built for the spread's favourite run. With five or six defenders in the box,
a defense can't afford to let inside zone's double teams climb to the linebackers. The
[**tite front**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tite-front) puts a nose on the center and two 4i-techniques
on the tackles' inside shoulders, so every interior lineman is covered and nobody climbs cleanly
([05-03](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd#the-tite-front-walling-off-the-middle)
draws it). Kirby Smart's Georgia calls the same picture the
[mint front](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mint-front), and Georgia's defenses won national titles in the
2021 and 2022 seasons with it as a base.[^georgia] It is also a case of parallel evolution rather than
borrowing: Vic Fangio's NFL defenses were running their own tite against the same spread run games, and the
two traditions met in the middle.

### Three-high: Iowa State's answer to the Air Raid

The newest answer came from the conference where the Air Raid lived. By 2017 the Big 12 was a league of spread
passing offenses, and Iowa State, under head coach Matt Campbell and defensive coordinator Jon Heacock, was
losing shootouts. After a 44–41 overtime loss to Iowa in the third game of 2017, Heacock and Campbell used
the bye week to throw out the playbook, and against Texas they lined up in a 3-3-5 with **three safeties
deep**. In the very next game Iowa State, a 31-point underdog with a walk-on backup quarterback, went to
Norman and beat third-ranked Oklahoma, Baker Mayfield's team, 38–31.[^isu]

A [**three-high safety defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-three-high-safety-defense) shows three
safeties deep before the snap, usually from a 3-3-5. It is built on one bet: **make the offense run the ball
against a light box, and fill the box late.**

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-high
#| fig-cap: "The three-high safety defense: one pre-snap picture, two answers. Before the snap: two 4i-techniques and a nose, the Mike behind them (four in the box), the Will and Sam at apex spots halfway to the slots, two cornerbacks, and three safeties (LS, FS, RS) 9 to 12 yards deep (receiver splits drawn a little tight to fit the page).
```
