Left, against a pass: eight drop (five deep, three under) and three rush, so four vertical routes run into five deep defenders and the quarterback settles for the check-down. Right, against inside zone: the receivers block the corners and the apex players, the Will squeezes, and the middle safety (ringed) flies down after the snap, so the box ends up with one more defender than it showed."
```{python}
def three_high_def():
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", -1), "4i"), D("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", 1), "4i"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -5.8, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 0.0, "M"), D("SAM", "SAM", 4.5, 5.8, "S"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB"),
            D("LS", "SS", 9.5, -9.5, "LS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, 0.0, "FS"), D("RS", "SS", 9.5, 9.5, "RS")]


def tight(players):
    """Narrow the spread for a half-page panel: wideouts and corners at 13 yards, slots at 8 (Air Raid splits vary)."""
    W = {"X": -13.0, "Z": 13.0, "H": -8.0, "F": 8.0, "LCB": -13.0, "RCB": 13.0, "LS": -8.6, "RS": 8.6,
         "WILL": -5.2, "SAM": 5.2}
    return [q.moved(w=W[q.key]) if q.key in W else q for q in players]


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 5.2))
# against the pass
p = Play(tight(spread10()), tight(three_high_def()), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, [(0, 0), (17.0, 0.4)])
for k in ("H", "F"):
    p.route(k, [(0, 0), (16.5, -0.6)])
p.route("RB", [(0, 0), (-0.4, 3.0), (1.5, 6.0)], side=-1)
p.dropback(2.0)
for k, end in [("LE", (-1.6, -3.4)), ("N", (-1.2, 0.6)), ("RE", (-1.6, 3.4))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "rush")
for k, end in [("LCB", (15.5, -13.4)), ("RCB", (15.5, 13.4)), ("LS", (15.0, -7.6)), ("RS", (15.0, 7.6)),
               ("FS", (16.0, 0.0)), ("WILL", (7.5, -6.6)), ("MIKE", (7.0, 0.0)), ("SAM", (7.5, 6.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "path")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-9.4, 19.6), title=False, numbers=True)
rb_end = (p.players["RB"].d + 1.5, p.players["RB"].w - 6.0)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-7.0, 0.0), rb_end, rad=0.2)
say(f, p, rb_end[0] - 3.4, rb_end[1] + 1.0, "check-down", color=style.BALL, fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 17.9, -3.8, "5 deep", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 10.4, -3.4, "3 under", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
panel_title(axes[0], "Pass: eight drop", size=8.8)
# against the run
p = Play(tight(spread10()), tight(three_high_def()), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LT", (0.6, -2.6), via=[(-0.3, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "LG", (0.6, -0.9), via=[(-0.3, -1.4)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.6, 0.3))
go_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 1.9), via=[(-0.3, 1.9)])
go_to(p, "RT", (2.6, 2.2), via=[(0.3, 3.4)])
go_to(p, "WILL", (3.4, -3.8), "path")                   # backside apex squeezes
go_to(p, "SAM", (3.9, 4.6), "path")                     # playside apex fits
go_to(p, "X", (5.4, -12.6), delay=0.1)                  # stalk the corners
go_to(p, "Z", (5.4, 12.6), delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "H", (3.0, -5.0), delay=0.1)                   # slots block the apex players
go_to(p, "F", (3.6, 5.6), delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "RB", (2.6, 1.4), "run", via=[(-4.3, -0.6), (-1.2, 1.2)])
go_to(p, "FS", (3.4, 1.2), "path")
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.1, 2.5), "path")
p.highlight("FS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-9.4, 19.6), title=False, numbers=True)
point_to(f, p, (16.4, 6.4), (8.0, 0.7), "the 'flyover':\nthe middle safety\nfills the run", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(axes[1], "Run: a safety flies down", size=8.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Why does that work against the Air Raid in particular? Because the Air Raid's whole menu is built to find
the hole in a two-high or one-high shell: the seam against Cover 3, the deep middle against Cover 2, the
crossers underneath against man. Against five deep defenders and three underneath, there is no deep hole, and
the offense's best answer, running the ball against a light box, is something many pure passing offenses
were least prepared to do. The cost is the run defense if the safety is late: count four in the box and two
apex players who may or may not get there, against five linemen and a running back with a head start. Iowa
State's version spread through the Big 12 and beyond (Kansas's offensive coordinator called Iowa State "the
originators"), and three-safety looks became a regular part of college defense.[^isu2] NFL defenses have
mostly borrowed the *personnel* (a third safety on the field, the [big
nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-big-nickel) of [A First Look at
Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)) and the habit of disguising the
shell before the snap ([06-06](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)), rather than
the full college package. The likely reason is the same filter as always: the bet only pays if a safety
arrives on time against NFL backs running behind NFL linemen, and a three-man rush gives an NFL quarterback
all day to find the soft spot underneath. The margins that make three-high work against a Big 12 Air Raid are
too thin on Sunday.

## Crossing over: how the ideas reached Sunday

Now set the lineages against the NFL's filter. The table puts each idea next to its route into the league
and what changed on the way.

| College idea | Where it peaked | How it reached the NFL | What the NFL kept | What it left behind |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Triple option (veer, wishbone, flexbone) | Houston, Texas, Oklahoma, 1965–1985; the academies since | It didn't, as a system | The idea of reading a defender | The hits on the quarterback, the three-back backfield |
| Wing-T | Delaware, 1950s–1990s; Malzahn's Auburn | Coaches' clinics; the jet-motion era (Rams, 49ers, late 2010s) | Series football, jet motion, buck sweep, the bootleg | The full under-center Wing-T backfield |
| BYU passing | BYU, 1972–2000 | People: McMahon, Young, Holmgren, Reid | Spacing and crossing routes | — (it was an ancestor) |
| Air Raid | Kentucky, Texas Tech, Oklahoma (Riley), 1997–2020 | Quarterbacks (Mahomes, Mayfield, Murray, Williams), then coaches (Kingsbury, 2019) | Mesh, shallow cross, Y-cross, four verticals; no-huddle | Very wide line splits, the near-absence of a run game |
| Spread option and zone read | West Virginia, Utah, Florida, 2001–2010 | Quarterbacks (Griffin, Kaepernick, Wilson, Newton, 2012; Jackson, 2018) | The zone read and its relatives as a package | A run game built *entirely* on the quarterback |
| Pistol | Nevada, 2005–2012 | Washington and San Francisco, 2012; Baltimore, 2019 | The formation, especially for running quarterbacks | — |
| Tempo | Oregon, Auburn, Baylor, 2009–2015 | Chip Kelly's Eagles, 2013 | No-huddle as an information tool | Tempo as a whole-game identity (it faded; see 08-04) |
| RPO | Everywhere, 2005–2015 | Reid's Chiefs and Pederson's Eagles, 2016–2018 | Quick-throw RPOs | Slower RPOs that need three yards for the linemen |
| Match quarters | Michigan State, Iowa, TCU, Alabama, 1995–2015 | Coaches (Fangio's tree, Staley), late 2010s | Two-high, split-field match coverage | — (it came home) |
| 3-3-5 stack, three-high | Memphis, West Virginia, Iowa State | Mostly hasn't | A third safety in nickel personnel; disguise | Three down linemen as a base |

: Ten college ideas through the NFL's filter. "Peaked" is approximate; the text and notes give dates and sources. {#tbl-crossing}

Three patterns run through @tbl-crossing.

**Players carry ideas better than coaches.** The ideas that crossed fastest arrived inside quarterbacks:
the zone read with Griffin, Kaepernick and Wilson in 2012, the Air Raid with Mahomes (a starter from 2018), the
designed quarterback run game with Lamar Jackson. NFL coaches built offenses around what their young
quarterbacks already knew how to do. College *head coaches* who tried to bring whole systems with them had a
much harder time. Steve Spurrier (Washington, 2002–2003), Nick Saban (Miami, 2005–2006), Chip Kelly
(Philadelphia, 2013–2015, then San Francisco), Urban Meyer (Jacksonville, 2021) and Matt Rhule (Carolina,
2020–2022) all left the NFL with losing or near-.500 records, none lasting more than four seasons, while ideas from their
college offenses and defenses stayed behind.[^coaches] The NFL takes the play and sends back the coach.

**The NFL adapts what it keeps.** The RPO crossed, but as a *quick-throw* RPO, because the one-yard rule
won't let linemen run-block while the quarterback waits. The zone read crossed, but as a few plays a game,
because the quarterback test is harsh. The Air Raid crossed, but inside offenses that also go under center,
use tight ends and run power. Every idea arrives a little smaller.

**The crossing has a rhythm.** Ideas arrive in waves when a generation of players makes them unavoidable,
and then the NFL's defenses answer and the wave recedes. The zone read surged in 2012 and receded by 2014
([Dynasties and Counterpunches](11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd) tells that story), though only the
quarterback *keep* receded: the shotgun handoff it had made respectable stayed, which is why the run line in
the chart below keeps climbing after 2014. The shotgun spread
rose for twenty years and has just started to give ground to the under-center game
([The Modern Era](11-05-the-modern-era.qmd)). Here is that long wave in data.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shotgun-imports
#| fig-cap: "The spread's long arrival: the share of NFL plays snapped from the shotgun, 1999–2025 (regular season), shown separately for passes (dropbacks, scrambles included) and runs, with some of the college imports of the text marked. The passing game moved to the shotgun first; the run game followed only once offenses learned to run from it, with zone reads, the pistol and RPOs. Shotgun runs went from about 2% of runs in 1999 to half of them in 2023, before the under-center revival of 2024–2025. The pistol is counted as shotgun in this data. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy (the `shotgun` flag)."
from gridiron.data import pbp

style.apply()
cols = ["season", "season_type", "play_type", "shotgun", "down", "qb_scramble"]
sg = pbp(list(range(1999, 2026)), columns=cols)
sg = sg[(sg["season_type"] == "REG") & sg["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & sg["down"].notna()].copy()
sg["kind"] = np.where((sg["play_type"] == "pass") | (sg["qb_scramble"] == 1), "pass", "run")
rate = sg.groupby(["season", "kind"])["shotgun"].mean().unstack() * 100
SG_ALL = sg.groupby("season")["shotgun"].mean() * 100

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.9))
ax.plot(rate.index, rate["pass"], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3)
ax.plot(rate.index, rate["run"], color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3)
ax.text(2025.4, rate.loc[2025, "pass"], "passes", color=style.SERIES[0], fontsize=8, va="center")
ax.text(2025.4, rate.loc[2025, "run"], "runs", color=style.SERIES[1], fontsize=8, va="center")
EVENTS = [  # season, series, label, label position (x, y), vertical alignment
    (2008, "run", "Wildcat (Dolphins,\nfrom Arkansas)", (2010.6, 1.5), "bottom"),
    (2012, "run", "read-option wave:\nGriffin, Kaepernick,\nWilson, Newton", (2015.4, 9.0), "bottom"),
    (2013, "pass", "Kelly's Eagles\n(Oregon tempo)", (2009.2, 86.0), "bottom"),
    (2018, "run", "RPO boom (2016-18):\nReid's Chiefs, the\nEagles' Super Bowl LII", (2019.8, 12.0), "bottom"),
    (2018, "pass", "Mahomes (Texas Tech)\nis NFL MVP", (2016.0, 93.0), "bottom"),
    (2023, "run", "peak: half of\nall runs", (2021.6, 60.0), "bottom"),
]
for yr, ser, txt, xy, va in EVENTS:
    ax.annotate(txt, (yr, rate.loc[yr, ser]), xytext=xy, fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, ha="center",
                va=va, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7, shrinkB=3))
ax.set_ylim(0, 105)
ax.set_xlim(1998.5, 2028.5)
ax.set_xticks(list(range(2000, 2026, 5)))
ax.set_ylabel("% of plays from the shotgun", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-shotgun-imports as two stories. The **passing** line is the spread formation arriving: from about
`{python} f"{rate.loc[1999, 'pass']:.0f}"`% of dropbacks in 1999 to `{python} f"{rate.loc[2009, 'pass']:.0f}"`%
in 2009, as offenses learned what college coaches had learned, that a quarterback who starts five yards deep
sees the defense better and gets the ball out faster. That shift needed no college import at all; the 2007
Patriots, the most famous spread passing offense of its era, were run by NFL lifers. The **running** line is
the college story. In 2011, only `{python} f"{rate.loc[2011, 'run']:.0f}"`% of NFL runs came from the
shotgun: the NFL used the gun to pass and went under center to run. That was a reasoned choice, and it
answers the question the timeline left open. [Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd#shotgun)
listed what the shotgun costs a run game: the back beside the quarterback takes the handoff moving sideways
rather than downhill, a five-yard snap can be fumbled, and play-action is less convincing when the
quarterback never turns his back. For a quarterback who never kept the ball, those costs bought nothing. The
zone read changed the arithmetic: once the quarterback's read made a shotgun run plus-one, the costs were
worth paying. Then the read-option wave and Chip
Kelly's Eagles arrived, and shotgun runs jumped to `{python} f"{rate.loc[2013, 'run']:.0f}"`% in 2013. The
spread run game, the zone read, the pistol and then the RPO, had crossed. By 2023 the shotgun accounted for
`{python} f"{rate.loc[2023, 'run']:.0f}"`% of runs and `{python} f"{SG_ALL.loc[2023]:.0f}"`% of all plays.
In 2025 both lines fell back (to `{python} f"{SG_ALL.loc[2025]:.0f}"`% of all plays), as NFL offenses went
back under center to run and play-action, the latest counterpunch, told in [The Modern Era](11-05-the-modern-era.qmd).
Two cautions: the play-by-play's `shotgun` flag comes from the official gamebook descriptions, which
probably recorded it less consistently in the early seasons, and it can't tell a spread-option shotgun run
from a plain shotgun handoff.[^data]

The borrowing hasn't stopped. Pre-snap motion, the Wing-T's oldest tool, was on 63.9% of NFL plays in 2025
by PFF's count, up from 37.6% in 2014,[^motion] and [The Modern Era](11-05-the-modern-era.qmd) follows what
is crossing now.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Washington at New Orleans, September 9, 2012"}
Robert Griffin III's first NFL game, a 40–32 win over the Saints, is this chapter's opening scene played for
real. Washington's attack "borrowed liberally from concepts Griffin used at Baylor," NFL.com reported that
week, and Mike Shanahan described how it worked: "we had running plays called and all of a sudden they gave
us certain looks to take the running game away, and we threw a couple of bubbles early."[^was2012]

**What to notice:** take one of those snaps apart and every piece has a college birthplace. The quarterback
four yards deep with the back behind him is Ault's pistol (Nevada, 2005); the unblocked backside end he reads
is Rodriguez's zone read (Glenville State, 1991); the bubble attached to it is West Virginia's third option;
and putting run and throw on one call is Baylor's packaged play. Then notice what Sunday changed: the bubble
comes out on the quarterback's first look, before any lineman can drift a yard downfield. The run side of
that offense is in [Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) and the packaged plays in
[Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd).
:::

## Saturday versus Sunday: the rules that shape each game

You can't watch a college game well without the rulebook differences, because many of the strategies in
this chapter exist *because* of them. Here they are side by side, current for the 2026 seasons. (The full
reference version lives in [Appendix E](../../appendices/appendix-e-rules-timeline-trees.qmd).)

| Rule | NFL (2026) | College (2026) | What it changes on the field |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Hash marks | 70 ft 9 in from each sideline; 18 ft 6 in apart | 60 ft from each sideline; 40 ft apart | College has a true wide side and short side on most snaps; formations and play calls are built around it |
| Catch at the sideline | Two feet (or another body part) in bounds | One foot (or any body part) in bounds | Sideline throws are easier to complete in college |
| Ineligible linemen downfield on a pass | No more than 1 yard, on any forward pass | No more than 3 yards, and only on passes that cross the neutral zone | College RPOs can run-block longer and throw deeper (Drill 3) |
| Defensive pass interference | Spot foul, automatic first down | 15 yards from the previous spot (or the spot, if shorter), automatic first down | A deep NFL throw into tight coverage can "win" 40 yards on a flag; in college the flag is capped |
| Offensive pass interference | 10 yards | 10 yards (15 until 2025) | Cut for 2026, matching the NFL |
| Clock after a first down | Keeps running | Stops only in the last two minutes of each half (stopped all game until 2023) | Pre-2023 college games had many more snaps; tempo offenses profited |
| Two-minute warning | Yes | Yes, since 2024 (the "two-minute timeout") | Late-half clock strategy now looks similar |
| Ball carrier down | When touched by an opponent while on the ground | As soon as a knee or other body part touches the ground, touched or not | No "get up and keep running" in college |
| Overtime | One 10-minute period in the regular season (15 in the playoffs); both teams get the ball; then sudden death | Alternating possessions from the 25; a two-point try is required after a touchdown from the second overtime; alternating two-point plays from the third | College overtime is a series of short-field possessions; strategy becomes two-point math |
| Targeting / hits to the head | 15 yards; ejection only for flagrant hits (use-of-helmet rule since 2018) | 15 yards and automatic ejection; for 2026, a first offense no longer carries a suspension into the next game | College defenders must change their tackling target or lose a starter |
| Kickoffs | The "dynamic kickoff" (since 2024), built to be returned | Traditional kickoff; a fair catch inside the 25 is a touchback at the 25 | Many college kickoffs end in a fair catch or a touchback |
| Fair-catch kick | Allowed for decades (rarely used) | New for 2026 | A free 3-point try after a fair catch near midfield, now in both games |
| Motion | One player, not moving forward at the snap | The same | Differences you see in motion are usage, not law |
| Helmet communication | Quarterback and one defender (green dot) since 1994 and 2008 | One player per side (FBS), since 2024 | College offenses used sideline signals and picture boards for decades, which is part of why tempo grew there |

: The college and NFL rules that most change strategy, as of the 2026 seasons. Sources in the notes below the table's discussion. {#tbl-rules}

A few of these deserve a sentence on *why* they matter.

**The hash marks** are the one you can see from your couch. With the ball on a college hash, offenses put
their strength into the wide field and leave a single receiver into the short side, and defenses set their
coverage by the field and the boundary rather than by the formation. That is why college defenses grew
field-and-boundary coverages (and split-field quarters, 06-06), and why college kickers sometimes waste a
down centering the ball before a field goal.[^hashrule]

**The three-yard rule, the one-foot catch and the capped DPI** all favour offenses that throw in rhythm off
the run and to the sideline; Drill 3 below puts the first two on one play.[^ncaarules] The NFL's
spot-foul DPI pushes the other way: it makes a deep throw into tight coverage a reasonable gamble, a strategy
[Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd)
measures.

**The college clock** change of 2023 (running after a first down except in the last two minutes of each
half) took away roughly seven or eight snaps a game, and the two-minute timeout followed for 2024.[^clock]
The college game has quietly moved toward the NFL's, and the tempo era's extra snaps are gone.

**Overtime** is a different sport in college. Since 2021, teams alternate possessions from the opponent's 25,
must go for two after a touchdown from the second overtime, and from the third overtime simply alternate
two-point plays.[^ot] The NFL's version is in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).

**Targeting** has made the college defender's aiming point a strategic question. A targeting foul ejects
the player; for 2026, in a one-year trial, a player's first targeting foul of the season no longer costs him
part of the next game, but second and third fouls still do.[^targeting] The NFL has no automatic ejection
for helmet contact.

**Kickoffs** have gone in opposite directions. The NFL rebuilt its kickoff in 2024 to bring the return back
([Kickoffs and Returns](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-02-kickoffs-and-returns.qmd)),
while college, since 2018, has let the receiving team fair-catch a kickoff inside its 25 for a touchback at
the 25, so many college kickoffs end in a touchback or a fair catch rather than a return.[^kickoff] For 2026 the NCAA also adopted the
[fair-catch kick](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fair-catch-kick), the old NFL rule that lets a team
attempt a free field goal from the spot of a fair catch.[^fck]

**Helmet communication** came to major college football only in 2024: one player per side with a speaker in his
helmet, cut off at 15 seconds on the play clock, as in the NFL.[^helmet] An offense that had always signalled
every play from the sideline lost nothing by going fast, which is one more reason tempo grew up on Saturday.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, every team in the league has roughly the same playbook menus, and so does every team in the
college game. Real college football is closer to a hundred different sports. On the same Saturday you can
watch a service academy run the flexbone triple option, an Air Raid team throw 60 times from five-receiver
sets, and an SEC power program line up under center with two tight ends. NFL teams are far more alike than
that, because they draw from the same talent pool under the same rules and copy each other within a season.
That variety is the laboratory. It's also why a college game is a good place to *see* a concept in its
purest form: the team that runs it is often the only one that does.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Saturday versus Sunday.** Watch one college game and one NFL game on the same weekend, and list three
structural differences you can see. Some places to look:

*Before the snap*

- **Where is the ball?** In college, on most snaps it sits on a hash 20 yards from one sideline. Which way
  does the offense put its receivers: into the wide field or the short side? Does the defense line up by
  the field and the boundary, or by the formation?
- **How fast is the next snap?** Time a few series from whistle to snap. College tempo teams snap in 10 to 15
  seconds; how many NFL teams do?
- **Who is in the backfield?** Count the formations with the quarterback under center. Then count the option
  looks (a back beside the quarterback, an unblocked end) and how often the quarterback actually keeps.
- **How many safeties are deep?** Look for college defenses with three safeties back, and for three-down-lineman
  fronts with stacked linebackers.

*After the snap*

- **On a run with a throw attached**, watch the offensive linemen: in college they may be two or three yards
  downfield when the ball is thrown. In the NFL, watch for the quick throw that comes out before they can
  get there.
- **On a sideline catch**, count the feet. One in college, two in the NFL.
- **On a long pass-interference flag**, where does the ball go? Fifteen yards in college; the spot of the foul
  in the NFL.

For your prediction log ([01-06](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)): on every college
option or RPO look, write who the quarterback is reading, and how many defenders are in the box against how
many blockers.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1: count the Saturday box.** First-and-10 at midfield in a Big 12 game. The ball is on the left hash.
The offense lines up in a four-receiver spread with the running back beside the quarterback. The defense
shows three down linemen, a Mike linebacker over the ball, the Will cheated in toward the box on the short
side, the Sam out over the slot on the wide side, and three safeties deep. Count the box against the
blockers. Is the offense more likely to run or pass, what kind of play, and what is the defense counting on?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: a four-receiver spread (10 personnel) against three-high, on a college field with the ball on the left hash (hash marks drawn at college width). The shaded strip is the box."
off = spread10()
ball_y = FIELD_WIDTH - 20.0          # the offense's left hash on a college field
OFF_W = {"X": -13.0, "H": -7.4, "Z": 20.0}
off = [q.moved(w=OFF_W[q.key]) if q.key in OFF_W else q for q in off]
DEF_AT = {"LCB": (7.0, -13.0), "RCB": (7.0, 20.0), "WILL": (4.5, -3.6), "SAM": (4.5, 8.2),
          "LS": (8.0, -6.5), "FS": (13.0, 2.0), "RS": (11.6, 11.0)}   # shaded to the field, by field and boundary
dfn = [q.moved(d=DEF_AT[q.key][0], w=DEF_AT[q.key][1]) if q.key in DEF_AT else q for q in three_high_def()]
check_legal(off)
with hashes_at(20.0):
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=60, ball_y=ball_y, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: 1st and 10, ball on the left hash")
    f = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 15.0), width_in=6.5)
clean(f.ax, numbers=True, hashes=False)
box_shade(f, p, -0.2, 7.0, -4.4, 4.4)
say(f, p, 12.0, -13.5, "short side:\n20 yards", fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.0, 25.0, "wide side: 33 yards", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-5.2, 17.6), (-3.0, 13.33), "college hash", fontsize=6.6, shrink=1)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Count it: five in the box against five blockers plus a read.** Three linemen, the Mike and the cheated-in
Will are in the box; the Sam is out over the wide-side slot. The offense has five linemen, and on a zone read
the quarterback reads one box defender instead of blocking him, so five linemen take the other four with one
to spare: **the offense is plus-one.** **Expect a run, most likely a read** (a zone read, or an RPO that
reads the Will), because the defense has invited it.

**What the defense is counting on** is the three safeties: on a run, one of them, usually the middle one,
comes down after the snap to fill, so the box gains a defender by the time the back gets there
(@fig-three-high). That's the bet of the three-high: give the offense a light box, take away everything deep,
and tackle the run late. If the safety is a step slow, the run is a big gain; if he's on time, the offense
has run into a six-man box it didn't see, and the plus-one is gone.

**Bonus: why you knew it was college.** The ball is 20 yards from the left sideline, not 23.6: college hash
marks. The offense put a receiver out on the numbers of a 33-yard wide side; the defense set its
safeties by field and boundary (the short-side safety tighter, the middle one shaded to the wide side, the
wide-side safety wider); and the three-safety shell is a college look.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2: the wishbone count.** A wishbone team runs the triple option to its split-end side (the
offense's left). On the first four snaps, the defense's left end (the 5-technique) has squeezed down hard on
the fullback every time, and the outside linebacker standing on the line outside him has run straight at
the pitch man every time. Before the next snap, name #1, #2, #3 and #4, and predict who will carry the ball.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: wishbone, triple option to the left. The two defenders who have been doing the same thing every snap are ringed; the prompt says what each has done."
p = Play(wishbone_off(), wishbone_def(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Drill 2: who carries it?")
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 11.5), window=(-6.8, 13.6), width_in=5.8)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**#1 is the 5-technique** (the dive key), **#2 the Will** standing on the line outside him (the pitch key),
**#3 the strong safety** in the alley (the lead halfback's block), and **#4 the cornerback** (the split end's
block). Use the quarterback's two reads in order:

1. **#1 squeezes the dive**, so the quarterback pulls the ball. The fullback carries out his fake and takes
   #1 with him.
2. **#2 widens to take the pitch man**, so the quarterback keeps and turns up inside him.

**The quarterback carries it**, up the seam between #1 (who is tackling a fullback with no ball) and #2 (who
is covering a halfback with no ball), with #3 and #4 blocked outside. A defense that does the same thing every
snap has stopped playing option defense, which is why wishbone teams ran the triple until a defender changed
his mind, and why defensive coaches, as [03-04](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd#how-defenses-answer-the-option)
showed, learned to mix up who took whom.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3: one play, two rulebooks.** An offense runs an RPO: the line run-blocks inside zone, and the
quarterback pulls the ball and throws to the slot receiver on a seam route that bends to the sideline. He
catches it 17 yards downfield, right at the sideline, with one foot down before stepping out. At the moment of the throw, the right guard, who came
off a double team toward a linebacker, is 2½ yards past the line of scrimmage, still not touching anyone.
What is the ruling in a college game? In an NFL game?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: the RPO at the moment of the throw. The shaded strips mark 1 and 3 yards past the line of scrimmage; the right guard's block ends between them. The slot receiver catches the ball at the sideline."
p = Play(spread10(), zrb_defense(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Drill 3: legal on Saturday? On Sunday?")
go_to(p, "LT", (0.45, -2.75), via=[(-0.3, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -1.2), via=[(-0.3, -1.4)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.45))
go_to(p, "RG", (2.5, 1.6), via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.7, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.55, 3.75))
p.route("F", [(0, 0), (11.0, -0.4), (18.5, 15.5)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 1.4), "path", via=[(-4.4, 0.0)])
p.pass_to("F", t=2.0)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-11.0, 26.6), window=(-6.8, 20.4), width_in=5.9)
box_shade(f, p, 0.0, 1.0, -11.0, 26.6, color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, alpha=0.18)
box_shade(f, p, 1.0, 3.0, -11.0, 26.6, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.06)
say(f, p, 0.5, 14.8, "NFL limit: 1 yard", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
say(f, p, 2.2, 14.8, "college limit: 3 yards", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
point_to(f, p, (-3.6, 5.6), (2.5, 1.6), "RG: 2½ yards\ndownfield", fontsize=6.6, shrink=2)
say(f, p, 11.6, 22.0, "caught with one\nfoot in bounds", fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**College: a legal 17-yard completion.** The guard is inside the three-yard limit, and a pass that crosses the
neutral zone is exactly what the college rule allows him to be up to three yards beyond. One foot in bounds
is a catch in college.

**NFL: no gain, and a flag.** The guard is more than a yard downfield when a forward pass is thrown, so it is
**illegal man downfield**: five yards from the previous spot, the completion erased, and the down replayed
([04-06](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd#the-one-yard-rule-why-nfl-rpos-look-different)). And even
without the flag, one foot in bounds isn't a catch in the NFL; the officials would rule it incomplete.

That's the whole reason NFL RPOs look different: the throw comes out in about a second, to a slant, a glance or
a bubble, before any lineman can drift a yard, and the deep seam that a college team runs off the same
action shows up on Sunday only as play-action, with the linemen pass-blocking.
:::

## Takeaways

- College football is the sport's laboratory because of its environment: **huge talent gaps** across hundreds
  of programs, **wide hash marks**, rules like the **three-yard** ineligible limit that tolerate the run-pass
  blur, and **roster churn and tempo** that reward small, repeatable systems.
- The offensive lineages share one aim, changing the arithmetic for the team with lesser players: the
  **option** (split-T, veer, wishbone, flexbone, spread option) reads a defender instead of blocking him; the
  **Wing-T** makes him guess; **BYU and the Air Raid** spread the ball to five receivers and repeat a few plays
  endlessly; the **spread offense** empties the box so the run game has numbers.
- The **spread option** is the triple option rebuilt from the shotgun, with the pitch replaced by a throw;
  add the three-yard rule and tempo and you have the modern college RPO offense.
- Defenses answered with **speed and disguise** (the 3-3-5 stack), **two-high match coverage** (quarters, which
  made a round trip back to the NFL), **fronts that wall off inside zone** (tite and mint) and **three-high
  safeties** that concede the light-box run and fill it late.
- The NFL is a filter: ideas that hit the quarterback, rely on a talent gap or need college rules arrive
  smaller or not at all. **Players carry ideas across better than coaches**, which is why the big crossings
  (2012's read option, 2017's RPOs, the Air Raid's concepts) came with young quarterbacks.
